review.notes: Resolved 2026-09-26: ENY-224 "Rat and Mouse Control" (Koehler & Kern, UF/IFAS) is back up at the FLVC/EDIS journal host (the ask.ifas.ufl.edu short URL still 404s, but the article record loads directly). It confirms: roof rats nest in attics/roof spaces/palm trees/shrubbery, are climbers, gnaw citrus fruit and are destructive to citrus groves, gnaw electrical wires/rafters in attics, and have a tail longer than the combined head and body, and that rats travel wires, pipes and rough walls using their sense of balance. Source URL added; ENY-224 re-verification note is resolved.

review.notes: Resolved 2026-09-26: ENY-224 (UF/IFAS, link above) confirms Norway rats are burrowers that dig under buildings/concrete slabs and along walls/rubbish (foundation-level activity). Its tail-length phrasing for Norway rats ("about as long as the combined head and body") is ambiguous next to the entry's "tail shorter than the body," so also checked icwdm.org (Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management, University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension), which states the Norway rat's tail "does not reach the tip of the nose" -- i.e., shorter than head+body -- and confirms ground-level burrowing near walls/buildings. Entry traits left as written; both URLs added to sources.

traits: Burrows along foundations and under slabs

Ground-floor and burrow specialist, rarely climbs high

review.notes: Resolved 2026-09-26: ENY-224 (UF/IFAS, link above) confirms house mice nibble at a wide variety of food sources (consistent with the "20-30 food sites a night" copy) and states mice can squeeze through a 1/4-inch crack ("any place a pencil can be poked, a mouse can go"), and gives dropping length as 1/8 inch (rice-grain sized, matching the entry). A 1/4-inch gap is narrower than a dime's diameter (~0.7 in), so the entry's "gap the width of a dime" is a true but more conservative comparison than the source's precise figure; left as written since it is not contradicted. Source URL added.

traits: Rice-grain-sized droppings in drawers and under sinks
Fits through a gap the width of a dime
Grayish-brown, much smaller than either rat species

look_alikes.difference: House mice are much smaller with rice-grain droppings; Norway rats are large with thick, capsule-shaped droppings and a burrow at ground level.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the droppings next to a coin for size.

copy.what_it_means: A mouse nibbles at 20-30 food sites a night rather than eating one big meal, which is why droppings show up in many places at once. One mouse is rarely just one — sealing dime-sized gaps helps keep the next one from using the same door.
